story.title: Chaining the Ships
story.text: The river is rough and the boats rock hard. Someone suggests chaining them together.
story.narration: On the Yangtze the wind was strong and the waves high. Cao Cao’s great ships rocked so badly that no one could stand steady on deck. Someone had an idea: use thick iron chains to tie the ships to one another, side by side. Linked into one broad raft, they would be as steady as dry land. In Romance of the Three Kingdoms this is the “chained ships”: each length of chain joins two ships, and those two join the next length — link by link. It is a story from a novel, not official history.

story.title: One Link After Another
story.text: Zhou Yu arranges his own side: one task, then the next, with no gap in between.
story.narration: On the other bank, Zhou Yu was making his own arrangements: first he sent people to see to the first task; the moment it was done, the second followed at once, then the third and the fourth. Only a short time lay between them — if the next task did not follow quickly once the one before was finished, the whole arrangement came apart and had to be begun again from the start. Laying the work out one thing after another, and linking it up link by link: that is the heart of the interlocking stratagem.

keyMoment.question: You are Zhou Yu: four tasks are laid out, to be carried through one after another. What matters most?

options.text: Do the first task, and the moment it is done start the second — never let a link fall empty
Start all four tasks at once and let whichever finishes first count
options.hint: Start them all at once and the order is lost — with the step before not yet laid, the step after cannot connect, and the whole arrangement scatters.

options.text: Do the last task beautifully first, and let the earlier ones wait
options.hint: The last task stands on the ones before it — leave those empty and the last has nowhere to rest.

keyMoment.reveal: Arrange one thing after another, with no gap — that is what holds it all together.

misconceptions: There is no harm in taking things slowly; a gap in the middle does not matter
Starting everything at once saves the most time
Order does not matter as long as everything gets done in the end

quiz.question: In Romance of the Three Kingdoms, why did Cao Cao chain his great ships together?
options: The river was rough and the ships rocked; chained together they were steady
He wanted the ships to sail faster
He wanted to hide the ships from view
quiz.explanation: In wind and waves the ships rocked so hard no one could stand; linked into one raft they were steady — that is where the chained ships came from.

quiz.question: What matters most in the interlocking stratagem?
options: Link after link, with no gap in between
The faster the better, whatever the order
Doing one single thing well is enough
quiz.explanation: Lay the work out one thing after another and link it up one ring at a time — break the middle and the road laid before it comes to nothing.

quiz.question: Your class is putting on a show, with one act after another on stage. What is the smoothest way?
options: Get the first act ready, start the next the moment it ends, and keep the later acts waiting backstage
Send every act on stage at once to do their own thing
Perform the last act first and worry about the rest later
quiz.explanation: Only link after link holds together — just as in the interlocking stratagem, the step before lays the road and the step after follows at once.

levelScript.breakLine: A link broke — light it from the shore again
